newsitem.title: GERMANY: Improved outlook seen for EU starch feed imports.
newsitem.headline: Improved outlook seen for EU starch feed imports.

text.p: Lower European Union imports of manioc, tapioca and molasses contributed to lower 1996 starch feeds imports but 1997 might bring larger imports at least of the latter two, German trader Alfred C Toepfer said.
Total starch feeds imports in 1996 were 11.3 million tonnes after 11.6 million in 1995.
The EU may be able to import four million tonnes of tapioca in 1997 after 3.2 million in 1996 because main producers Thailand, Indonesia and China harvested bigger crops.
The 1996 figure represented less than 50 percent of the possible EU import quota, Toepfer said, citing a number of factors.

Origin farmers had switched area from tapioca to sugar cane and Thailand had made conscious efforts to be less dependent on the EU by exploring other tapioca export channels, for example South Korea and Indonesia.
But a faster pace of exports into the EU, for arrival in the Netherlands, was expected in the first half of 1997.
But Toepfer noted the tapioca/soymeal feed combination had to compete with inexpensive feed grains.
Soybeans prices needed to sink under Latin American harvest pressure to become competitive, it said.
Alternatively, good EU rapeseed prospects in 1997 could help ease high oilseeds prices and this would favour of the competitiveness of tapioca/soymeal.
EU molasses imports in 1997 should rise from 3.70 million tonnes in 1996 (3.74 million 1995), but Toepfer did not offer a precise forecast.
It expected higher shipments from Pakistan, Thailand and Indonesia although main supplier India was expected to produce less sugar cane.
Poland was also expected to export more molasses while the key producer in eastern Europe, the Ukraine, only harvested a disappointing beet crop.
Molasses, the syrup remaining after sugar separated by crystallisation is removed during refining, is the most important starch feed in the EU which is also the largest molasses consumer.
Because of oversupply in 1996, prices cif Rotterdam fell to $96 from $130 in the course of the year, boosting consumption.
